UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY
FINANCIAL CRIMES ENFORCEMENT NETWORK
IN THE MATTER OF No. 2001 - 02
ANGELINA PLETT
ASSESSMENT OF CIVIL MONEY PENALTIES
AGAINST ANGELINA PLETT
I. INTRODUCTION
The Secretary of the United States Department of the Treasury has delegated to
the Director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (“FinCEN”) the authority to
determine whether a financial institution has violated the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C.
§§5311 et seq. and 31 CFR Part 103 thereunder (“BSA”), and what, if any, sanction is
appropriate.
II. JURISDICTION
Angelina Plett (“Plett”) was, at all relevant times, an owner and the manager of
Cash For Checks Inc. (“Cash For Checks”). Cash For Checks was, at all relevant times, a
licensed check casher located in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma and was a “financial
institution” within the meaning of 31 U.S.C. §5312(a)(2) and 31 CFR §103.11(n).1
III. FINCEN’S DETERMINATIONS
A. Structuring
FinCEN has determined that between July 11, 1995, and April 26, 1996, Plett
willfully structured or willfully assisted in structuring check cashing transactions for
Joseph A. Sivigliano (“Sivigliano”) through a domestic financial institution in violation
of 31 U.S.C. §5324(a)(3) and 31 CFR §103.63(c). During the relevant time period,
Sivigliano cashed 136 checks totaling more than $1.17 million at Cash For Checks. On
each of 43 days, Sivigliano cashed a series of checks that individually totaled less than
$10,000, but that together exceeded $10,0

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5324?
statutory.answer: Neutral: 31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring to evade CTR reporting, but the facts show only multiple sub-$10,000 cash deposits and do not establish intent to evade or that the deposits were structured to avoid a required report.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5324(a) makes it unlawful to (1) structure or assist in structuring, or attempt to structure, any transaction with one or more domestic financial institutions, (2) for the purpose of evading the reporting requirements of 31 U.S.C. § 5313(a) (CTR reporting), and also prohibits causing or attempting to cause a financial institution to fail to file a required report (§ 5324(a)(1)) or to file a report with a material omission/misstatement (§ 5324(a)(2)). Here, the fact pattern shows ten cash deposits ranging from ~$5,289 to ~$9,858 labeled “sub-CTR cash deposit,” which is consistent with transactions that could be structured below the $10,000 CTR threshold and thus could satisfy the ‘structuring’ act element under § 5324(a)(3) if done to evade reporting. However, § 5324 requires a purpose/intent element—‘for the purpose of evading’ CTR reporting—and the facts do not provide evidence of intent (e.g., statements, instructions to bank staff, patterns tied to a single day exceeding $10,000 at one institution, or other indicia that the deposits were broken up to avoid a CTR rather than reflecting ordinary restaurant cash receipts across days/locations). The record also does not establish that any CTR was actually required and avoided (e.g., multiple same-day deposits aggregating over $10,000 at the same financial institution) or that the entity caused a bank to fail to file a required report under § 5324(a)(1). Therefore, while the pattern is suspicious, the available facts are insufficient to conclude the conduct falls within § 5324; ‘31 U.S.C. § 5324 prohibits structuring’ but intent to evade is not established on these facts.
